title: Selvage Session Protocol — the sealed payloads that are JSON, and the vocabulary a refused frame is reported in
description: `selvage/2`'s binary frame is an envelope of bytes, not a JSON frame, and its layout is CANONICAL.md §6.1's; what the envelope carries sealed is either opaque y-protocols bytes or one of these four objects. Valid against PROTOCOL.md §7.1: the room state the host publishes, the closing that ends the room, the holds a connection announces and the session-key announcement a connection makes about itself. None is a session frame — none carries `v` — and each is canonical when it follows CANONICAL.md §2, `listing` in the order §2.7 gives it, with §3's tolerance for a member the receiver does not know. Every object here tolerates a member it does not know, as every schema in this directory does. `refusalReason` is the thing this file fixes that is not a payload: the local report a receiver answers a refused frame with, which no frame carries and which `PROTOCOL.md` §13.2 binds a client to produce.

refusalReason.title: the reason a refused frame is reported in
refusalReason.description: The receiver's local report, and the check order it is read in: CANONICAL.md §6.1's table, whole. A frame is refused for the first of these that applies to it, and PROTOCOL.md §13.2 requires a client to report the reason rather than drop a frame silently. It is a closed *value* rather than a member — no frame carries it, and a receiver tolerates a member it does not know (§3) — so this is the one place in this file where a string an implementation invents is refused. `bad_tag` is the reason a reader would expect and cannot have: the signature covers the ciphertext, so a flipped tag byte reaches a verifier as a signature failure and no conforming receiver can report a tag failure at all (CANONICAL.md §6.1; `docs/studies/peer-corpus.md` §5.4 measured it). `unauthorised_content` is the one reason here that is not a property of the envelope: an authentic frame from a key the host's state gives role `viewer` carrying document content is refused by the peer rules (PROTOCOL.md §13.5). `bad_payload` is the one reason about the plaintext: an authentic frame whose plaintext is not an object of the members its `kind` fixes with each member of the type that kind gives it, which no reason about the envelope reaches (CANONICAL.md §6.1 step 8). A *value* of the right type that a rule elsewhere governs is not read at step 8 and is not this reason: a listing's path or a holds' path that `PROTOCOL.md` §5 refuses is dropped by the receiver and refuses neither the frame nor the state (§13.3, §13.7).

sealedIssued.description: The host's edition of a sealed value: the room state's `issued`, and the `issued` a closing carries above every state the host has published. A count, in CANONICAL.md §2.4's form and inside its bound, because the receiver that compares it against the highest it has accepted may be a JavaScript one. It orders the two values the host signs; a frame's `counter` orders the frames one key signs, and the two are different numbers with different jobs (CANONICAL.md §6.1). The lower bound is what a count is and not where `0` is refused: a negative value is not a count, so step 8 refuses it `bad_payload`, while `0` is a count and a receiver's mark starts there, so a state or a closing at `0` is refused `stale_issued` at step 9, where the value is read. The first state a host publishes therefore carries `1`, above the mark (CANONICAL.md §6.1, PROTOCOL.md §7.1).

sealedRole.description: The role the host assigns to a key in the room state: `host`, `guest`, or `viewer`, the role the host denies a peer's edits to. It is a fact the host states and signs, and no server seats it: a role binds to a key, and it is the host's to assign (`PROTOCOL.md` §1.2, §7.1, §13.4). What a receiver does with a key it commits as `viewer` is `PROTOCOL.md` §13.5's: it refuses document content from that peer and reports it `unauthorised_content`, while its SyncStep1 and its awareness are answered and applied.

declaredRole.description: The role a client may declare in its session-key announcement: `guest` or `viewer`, and never `host`. A state names exactly one `host` entry and it is the host's own connection's, so `host` is not a role a peer can declare for itself; a conforming host honours a declaration when it first commits that key, and a declaration about a key the state already commits changes that key's role not at all (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). What a role is enforced by is the clients that conform to it (§13.5).

sealedPeerKey.description: A peer's public key: the name of its entry in the room state's `peers`, and the value a session-key announcement carries. 32 bytes of Ed25519 in the encoding the invite URL's fragment writes one in — base64url, RFC 4648 §5, unpadded, so exactly 43 characters and no escape in a canonical JSON string (CANONICAL.md §2.3). The last character carries four bits of the value and two that are zero (RFC 4648 §3.5), so it is one of `AEIMQUYcgkosw048`: a 43-character string whose last character is any other spells no 32-byte value, and a receiver refuses it `bad_payload` at CANONICAL.md §6.1's step 8 rather than resolving it to one a strict decoder would not — two spellings of one key are one key only to a lenient reader, and this file is where the two ends of a connection agree. The length is pinned twice on purpose: `$` in a `pattern` may match before a trailing newline in some engines — Python's `re` is one — so a 43-character key with one appended would pass the pattern alone, and `minLength`/`maxLength` are what refuse it. The key itself and not its 8-byte id: an id is something a receiver derives (SHA-256 of these 32 bytes, first 8) and an id alone verifies nothing, so a state that named one would commit nothing anyone could check.

sealedPeer.description: One seat as the host's state records it, under the peer's public key as the member name. Nothing authoritative here is a value the server supplies: the key is the peer's own and the role is the host's, while `peer_id` is a label the host wrote about a name the server minted, and no rule in either document rests any authority on it (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.4).

peer_id.description: The seat the host believes this key's holder is seated under. It is what a client reads to answer a question about presence — whether the state's `host` entry is seated (PROTOCOL.md §13.8), whether a key's holder has left (§13.7) — and it decides no attribution and no role (§13.4). A host commits every announcement it accepts and labels the entry with the seat it believes holds the key or with any seat the roster names, because a missing label would leave the peer's whole session uncommitted while a wrong one costs only the presence questions (§7.1).

roomState.title: the sealed room state
roomState.description: The host's whole statement about a room, published sealed under the frame key with kind 1 and signed by the host key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). It replaces the receiver's previous state wholesale: a shorter `listing` is a smaller working tree and not a partial update.

listing.description: The host's working tree as it enumerated it: paths, carrying no content, each a candidate rather than a promise of a readable file. Written ascending by UTF-16 code unit (CANONICAL.md §2.7), which is the only order `selvage/2` promises. Each path is held to `PROTOCOL.md` §5's rule for one, and that rule is not read here: a receiver that will not carry a path *drops the path* and applies the rest of the listing and the state's roles, refusing neither the frame nor the state, so this member is held to step 8's member set and types and not to the value of each path (`PROTOCOL.md` §13.3, CANONICAL.md §6.1).

peers.description: The roster the host seats, **by public key**, the host's own entry included: the role each key is given and the seat the host believes it is held at. Keyed by the key rather than by `peer_id`, because `peer_id` is the server's word and a role bound to it would be a role any peer could claim by claiming the name (PROTOCOL.md §13.4). An object rather than `room.joined`'s array of the same name, because this one is looked up by key and not listed. One key cannot appear under two names, so the two errors left are one `peer_id` under two keys and two `host` roles: a receiver reads the entry whose key comes first in UTF-16 code-unit order, so two conforming receivers read one state the same way (CANONICAL.md §6.1).

roomClosing.title: the sealed closing
roomClosing.description: The host's statement that a room is over, published sealed under the frame key with kind 2 and signed by the host key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). One member is a constant and the other is what makes a replay of an old closing a drop rather than an end: a closing is ordered by `issued`, above every state the host has published.

closing.description: Constant. The kind is already what makes this a closing; the member is what a reader of the plaintext sees, and what keeps the payload an object rather than an empty one.

roomHolds.title: the sealed holds
roomHolds.description: The paths one connection keeps open, published sealed under the frame key with kind 3 and signed by that connection's session key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.7). It is a peer's own statement about itself, so no member here names the peer it is about: the sender is the key that signed the frame, and a receiver attributes the set by the verification it already made (`CANONICAL.md` §6.1). The set is leased rather than held by the server, which relays it and reads nothing in it.

holds.description: The set of paths the sender holds open, replaced wholesale by the next holds message under the same key. A set, so no order is promised (`CANONICAL.md` §2.7), and each path is held to `PROTOCOL.md` §5's rule as a listing's is — read at the receiver and not here: a receiver **drops** a blank or control-carrying path from the set it keeps for that peer, and refuses neither the message nor the session (`PROTOCOL.md` §13.7, `CANONICAL.md` §6.1).

sessionAnnouncement.title: the sealed session-key announcement
sessionAnnouncement.description: The one thing that makes a peer's key knowable to the room: a `kind = 4` frame, sealed under the frame key and **signed by the very key it announces**, which is why a receiver verifies a frame of this kind against the value inside it rather than against a key it already holds (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.1; CANONICAL.md §6.1's order for this kind). It is the only binary frame a client may send before a room state commits its key.

key.description: The announcing connection's session public key, and the key that signed the frame: the envelope's `key_id` must be its 8-byte id, and the signature must verify against it. Nothing binds it to a `peer_id`, which is the point — a claim about a server-assigned name is a claim any peer could make about another's.

role.description: The role the sender believes it has been given. Optional, and the one statement about a peer's role that comes from the peer's own key; a conforming host honours it when it first commits that key, and a later declaration about a key the state already commits leaves that key's role as the state has it (PROTOCOL.md §7.1).
